answer: Neighborhood pruning: each identity may hold at most k live peer edges, and edge renewal requires the counter endpoint to have previously served it in a distinct transaction. An ember of trust thus needs reciprocal history, not just a keypair. Sybils must fund k real counterparties per node, so cost scales with genuine service, not registrations. A falcon's reach stays wide; new clusters get pruned until saffron-marked activity deepens edges.
